concepts.name: Punch-Marked Coins (PMCs): Origins and Classification
key_dimensions: Debate over earliest issuance: Janapada vs. Imperial origin (6th–4th century BCE)
Silver vs. copper PMCs — relative chronology and geographical distribution
Symbols punched (sun, six-armed symbol, hill, elephant) and their interpretive controversies
UPSC trap: PMCs are NOT attributed to any single dynasty with certainty — distinguishing Mauryan PMCs from pre-Mauryan ones

concepts.name: Uninscribed vs. Inscribed Coinage: Transitional Significance
key_dimensions: PMCs as uninscribed coins — limitations in attribution and dating
Transition to inscribed coins under Indo-Greek rulers as a numismatic revolution
Significance of bilingual/biscript coins (Greek + Kharosthi/Brahmi) for historical reconstruction
UPSC trap: First truly inscribed coins in Indian subcontinent linked to Indo-Greeks, NOT Mauryas

concepts.name: Indo-Greek Coinage: Numismatic Firsts
key_dimensions: Introduction of portraiture (realistic royal portraits) — a first in Indian numismatic history
Bilingual legends: Greek on obverse, Kharosthi/Brahmi on reverse
Hellenistic artistic influence vs. Indian iconographic adaptation
Role as primary historical evidence for reconstructing Indo-Greek dynastic succession (e.g., Menander I)

concepts.name: Mauryan Monetary System and State Control
key_dimensions: Arthashastra evidence: Lakshanadhyaksha (Superintendent of Coins) — state monopoly over mint
Rupa (silver PMC) as standard unit; Pana, Masaka, Kakini as subdivisions
Counterfeiting laws and punishment described in Arthashastra — UPSC trap on official vs. private minting
Debate: Whether Mauryan empire had a fully monetized economy or mixed barter-coin system

concepts.name: Satavahana Coinage: Regional Numismatic Identity
key_dimensions: Use of lead, potin (copper-tin alloy), and copper — absence of gold coins as significant
Bilingual coins (Prakrit + Telugu/Tamil scripts in later issues) reflecting Deccan multilingualism
Ship motif on coins as evidence of maritime trade activity
UPSC trap: Satavahanas primarily used lead coins — contrast with contemporaneous gold-rich Kushana coinage

concepts.name: Kushana Gold Coinage (Dinara): Economic and Religious Significance
key_dimensions: Introduction of large-scale gold coinage (dinara) — influenced by Roman aureus
Syncretic religious imagery: Greek (Helios), Iranian (Mithra), Hindu (Shiva), and Buddhist motifs on same dynasty's coins
Kanishka I coins as evidence for dating debates (Kanishka era controversy)
Kushana gold standard's role in facilitating Silk Route trade — monetization of long-distance commerce

concepts.name: Gupta Coinage: Typology and Artistic Apex
key_dimensions: Seven standard coin types: Archer, Horseman, Tiger-slayer, Lyrist, etc. — each linked to specific rulers
Gupta gold coins (Dinaras) as evidence for political legitimacy and royal ideology
Decline of Gupta coinage quality in later period as indicator of economic/political decline
UPSC trap: Samudragupta's 'Lyrist type' coin as evidence for his personal accomplishments vs. propagandistic interpretation

concepts.name: Roman Coin Finds in India: Evidence for Trade Networks
key_dimensions: Hoards at Pudukottai, Coimbatore, Akenpalle — geographic concentration in South India
Augustus and Tiberius era coins most common — peak of Indo-Roman trade (1st century BCE–2nd century CE)
Defacement/countermarking of Roman coins for local circulation vs. use as bullion
UPSC trap: Roman coins indicate TRADE, not Roman political control — misinterpretation to avoid

concepts.name: Sangam-Age South Indian Coinage
key_dimensions: Chera, Chola, Pandya coins — distinct symbols (bow, tiger, fish) as dynastic identifiers
Predominantly copper/lead coins; limited gold usage — contrast with North Indian contemporaries
Sangam literature (Purananuru, Akananuru) as corroborating textual evidence
Rasi coins (punch-marked types) of Tamil kingdoms — overlap with North Indian PMC tradition

concepts.name: Coin Metallurgy as Economic Indicator
key_dimensions: Debasement of coinage (reducing silver/gold content) as indicator of fiscal stress — Post-Gupta period
Shift from silver PMCs → copper → lead → potin across different periods and regions
Karshapana standard (weight-based silver unit) and its variations across Janapadas
UPSC trap: Debasement ≠ end of monetary economy; it signals inflation/crisis, not abandonment of coinage

concepts.name: Janapada and Mahajanapada Coinage: Pre-Mauryan Diversity
key_dimensions: Regional variation: Gandhara, Kosala, Magadha, Kashi PMC types — identified by punch symbols
Evidence that coinage emerged from merchant guilds (Shrenis) before state control
Transition from barter (Nishka, Satamana — weighed metal) to coined money
UPSC trap: Nishka and Satamana in Vedic texts are NOT coins but weighed gold/silver pieces — pre-coin monetary units

concepts.name: Western Kshatrapa (Shaka) Coinage: Administrative Evidence
key_dimensions: Long dynastic series of silver coins with regnal years — unique dating system enabling precise chronology
Bilingual (Greek script vestige + Brahmi) showing cultural transition over time
Coin evidence for Chastana as founder — numismatics resolving textual ambiguity
Comparison with Kushana contemporaries: Silver-dominant vs. Gold-dominant economies

concepts.name: Buddhist and Religious Iconography on Coins
key_dimensions: Dhamma Chakra, Bodhi tree, triratna symbols on post-Mauryan coins (Shunga, Satavahana)
Absence of Buddha's human image on early coins — aniconic tradition in numismatics
Kushana coins showing Buddha in human form — earliest numismatic evidence of Buddhist anthropomorphism
UPSC trap: Human Buddha image appears on Kushana coins BEFORE it becomes common in sculpture — numismatic precedence debate

concepts.name: Guild (Shreni) Coinage and Private Minting
key_dimensions: Evidence of merchant guild-issued coins (e.g., Takshashila copper coins with guild marks)
Arthashastra provisions regulating private coinage alongside state minting
Guild coins as evidence for autonomous commercial institutions in ancient India
UPSC trap: Not all ancient Indian coins were state-issued — guild/civic coinage existed, complicating attribution

concepts.name: Coin Evidence for Reconstructing Political History
key_dimensions: Indo-Greek kings known ONLY through coins (e.g., Antimachus, Apollodotus) — no textual records
Overstruck coins revealing political succession and conquest (e.g., Kushana overstriking Parthian coins)
Coin hoards as evidence for political disruption, invasion, and economic hoarding behavior
UPSC trap: Coins as PRIMARY source vs. CORROBORATIVE source — methodological hierarchy in historical reconstruction

concepts.name: Weight Standards and Metrological Systems
key_dimensions: Karshapana (32 rattis = ~3.3g silver) as pan-Indian standard for PMCs
Suvarna/Nishka as gold weight standard in Mauryan system (Arthashastra)
Regional deviations from standard weights — Taxila standard vs. Magadha standard
UPSC trap: Ratti (Abrus precatorius seed ~0.11g) as the base unit — biological standardization of ancient weights

concepts.name: Post-Gupta Coinage Decline and the 'Dark Age' Debate
key_dimensions: Drastic reduction in coin finds between 7th–9th centuries CE — 'monetization reversal' hypothesis
Return to barter/grain-based transactions in early medieval period — feudalism debate (D.D. Kosambi vs. R.S. Sharma)
Regional continuity: South Indian coinage continues despite North Indian decline
UPSC trap: Absence of coins ≠ absence of trade — temple economy and land grants as alternative exchange mechanisms

concepts.name: Numismatic Sources vs. Literary/Epigraphic Sources: Methodological Comparison
key_dimensions: Coins as unintentional historical evidence (less prone to royal bias than inscriptions)
Limitations: Coins cannot explain motives, policies, or social conditions in detail
Complementarity: Allahabad Pillar inscription + Samudragupta's coin types — corroborating military campaigns
UPSC trap: Numismatics is classified under ARCHAEOLOGY, not epigraphy — source classification questions

concepts.name: Indo-Parthian and Indo-Scythian (Shaka) Coinage: Cultural Synthesis
key_dimensions: Maues (earliest Shaka king) coins — bilingual, showing continuity with Indo-Greek tradition
Gondophares coins and their link to Christian tradition (St. Thomas legend) — historiographical controversy
Gradual Indianization of coin types: Iranian/Greek motifs replaced by Indian deities over time
UPSC trap: Indo-Parthians and Indo-Scythians are DISTINCT groups often confused — Gondophares = Indo-Parthian, NOT Shaka
